title: forced labour will eus threat product bans succeed where supply chain audits  ecmii 2026 09 03
text:
September 2 - From December next year, companies face losing access to the European Union if their products are found to have been made with forced labour. The EU’s Forced Labour Regulation will provide belt and braces to its Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, where companies in scope must identify, prevent, mitigate and account for adverse human rights and environmental impacts in their operations, subsidiaries and value chains.
While campaigners say effective enforcement of the forced labour regulation will require the European Commission and EU member states to significantly boost their investigative capacity, the prospect of product bans could be the stick that will encourage companies to carry out due diligence required under the CSDDD.
What is clear is that voluntary due diligence approaches by companies have not succeeded in eliminating forced labour and other human rights abuses from global supply chains, despite the fact they have spawned a social auditing industry valued at $19.36 billion.
Around the world, 27.6 million people are estimated to be the victims of forced labour, and 63% of them in the private economy. Human rights groups say wage theft, unsafe working conditions and harassment are widespread, with migrants and other vulnerable workers especially affected.
Critics of the due diligence systems include suppliers, who complain of audit fatigue, and labour rights groups, who arguing that third-party assessments fail to capture the full picture, either because the audits are too superficial, too short, or because workers feel intimidated.
Neil Willings, global head of sustainability and supply chain at global compliance ​company SGS, insists that robust and diligent auditing offers companies a “solid baseline” about suppliers’ current performance as well as identifying areas for improvement.
He also rejects a common assumption that supplier audits are laxer for being voluntary. He cites the 10-year-old Association of Professional Social Compliance ​Auditors (APSCA) as evidence of the sector’s robustness. Set up by the likes of Bureau Veritas, Intertek and SGS, the industry body now counts over 75 verified members, including most of the world’s major social audit ⁠providers.
“There are still some pockets where industries choose to ignore bad practices. But looking back over the decades, a lot of progress has been made to improve supply chain compliance and reduce the risk of worker abuses,” he asserts.
But Aruna Kashyap, associate director in the economic justice ​and rights division at campaign group Human Rights Watch, says most due diligence practices only look at one side of the story.
“Companies are reluctant to look at the actual commercial drivers that often underpin labour abuses, like how contract prices are set or how fast orders have to be ​turned around. It’s as if social audits are almost set up to fail.”
A new study, meanwhile, suggest that due diligence mechanisms are less important than the buyer-supplier relationships that sit above them.
Based on historic 2018 audit data from the U.S. fast fashion brand GAP, the study, in the Strategic Management Journal, found that suppliers were more likely to comply with social requirements specified by GAP when they were in longer-term commercial relationship with the brand. Suppliers that faced high competition within their product category also proved more amenable to changing their practices.
Even more influential, however, is when there was a “threatened penalty” for failure to meet core labour standards: in this case, ​the loss of business.
GAP’s initial policy was to work with low-performing suppliers to encourage them to improve, but it then introduced the threat of cutting commercial ties if suppliers failed to improve fast enough.
The result was marked: an improvement by 0.8 standard deviations in supplier’s compliance scores and ​a 22-percentage-point fall in the probability of them failing their next audit. Without it, suppliers showed “no improvement” when they failed to meet GAP’s compliance requirements.
The fashion giant’s policy today strikes the same balance, a company spokesperson confirmed. “Gap Inc is committed to supporting factory partners through remediation if we identify non-compliances, but in ‌some instances violations ⁠of our code of vendor conduct can result in termination of commercial relations.”
Matthew Amengual, an associate professor at Oxford University’s Saïd Business School and co-author of the paper, says the research provides at least three major takeaways. First, for voluntary approaches to work, buyers need to “show that they are serious”, by integrating corporate procurement and buying divisions into the compliance process.
If the sole message from a purchasing department remains on quality and cost, they are unlikely to take on board injunctions from the compliance department about social rights.
The second lesson is that relationships trump rules every time. If a supplier knows that a buyer won’t “cut and run”, either at the first hint of non-compliance or because of a lower-cost offer elsewhere, then the motivation to invest in social compliance measures is far higher, says Amengual.
It’s a sentiment echoed by Arianna Rossi, senior research and policy coordinator at the ​International Labour Organization (ILO), who argues that a policing approach is less needed ​when buyers and suppliers know and trust one another.
Buyers can ⁠foster such relationships not only through longer-term contracts or participation in joint labour accords, but also through financial or technical support for action plans put in place by suppliers to improve social standards.
Rossi cites the example of ACT for Cambodia, a “supply-chain supported” initiative between trade unions, suppliers and purchasing brands to encourage collective bargaining agreements in the country’s fashion and footwear sector.
“The kind of dialogue and opportunities to exchange ideas that a multistakeholder ​platform like this offers is really critical to helping brands hear the perspective of suppliers and workers, as well as to finding practical solutions to the problems behind instances of non-compliance,” she explains.
Importantly, ​such a strategy turns penalties into a ⁠signal of intent to external stakeholders, who might otherwise interpret a buyer’s willingness to collaborate as condoning poor practice in its supply chain.
The third takeaway relates to the limitations of voluntary mechanisms, particularly when it comes to the power imbalance between suppliers and buyers.
Corporations are not blind to this, with responsible buyers encouraging measures such as whistleblowing and confidential employee interviews to give more voice to workers. A case in point is EcoVadis’s Ulula service, which, among other functions, provides workers with a confidential channel to report abuses and seek remediation via their mobile phones.
“Triangulating the information that suppliers provide with what workers provide ⁠is a good ​way to really get to the bottom of things and also to validate (audits, which) are a snapshot in time … What we can do here is something that happens much ​more continuously,” explains Antoine Heuty, founder of Ulula and senior vice-president of human rights at EcoVadis.
Amengual also sees merit in toughening the transparency criteria of mandatory due diligence laws so they include consistent reporting on outcomes of mitigation efforts, such as how often contracts are cancelled due to non-compliance or whether remediation plans increase compliance, he says.
At present, such ​data is almost impossible to obtain, Amengual states. Either companies don’t have the internal systems to offer an accurate picture, or, where they do have the data, they are reluctant to share it. As he notes: “No company wants to say, ‘Oh, we've gotten slightly better in our human rights violations’.”
